title: Intel ( INTC ) might expand its gaming focus beyond the PC m

organizations.name: radeon technology group of advanced micro devices

text:
Intel ( INTC ) might expand its gaming focus beyond the PC market. NPD Group’s most recent report said U.S. gamers bought more than 1 million units of video game consoles in January 2018. Last month’s gaming hardware sales in the U.S. was $278 million, up +119% Y/Y. Supplying processors for gaming consoles is an ideal expansion move for Intel’s custom foundry business .
This is not purely speculative. Read between the lines, do not be myopic. Intel's November 8, 2017 hiring of Raja Koduri as senior vice-president for the newly-formed Core and Visual Computing group is a clue to its expanded ambition. Before November 8, Koduri was the chief of Radeon Technology Group of Advanced Micro Devices ( AMD ).
He went back to AMD in April 2013, just in time to head the team that developed the Jaguar APU processors for Sony's ( SNE ) processor. Koduri is obviously an expert in creating custom processors.
Intel doesn't sell discrete video cards. Koduri did not get hired to help Intel build discrete GPUs so that it could compete with Nvidia ( NVDA ) and AMD's Radeon or GeForce video cards. Koduri was hired to improve Intel's CPU/GPU System-on-Chips. The advances in the custom Accelerated Processing Unit [APU] designs of AMD is why console hardware manufacturers use AMD Jaguar processors.
Even Apple ( AAPL ) with its lucrative iPhone business recently updated its trademark (covering 60 countries) with a renewed focus on gaming consoles and peripherals. It is high time that Intel builds on the idea originated by the handheld gaming console below.
